title: capacity-optimizer-scenarios-and-simulation-notes
body:
Purpose:
This is a working note for a lightweight capacity optimizer used to evaluate continuous batching + concurrency sizing across realistic arrival shapes. Goal: give product and SRE practical knobs and a small spreadsheet/sim that maps target p95 and cost per 1M tokens to concurrency, batch-window, and headroom factors.

Summary of approach (short):
- Build a discrete-event simulator (fast, vectorized) that models request arrivals, per-request token lengths, batching windows, and multi-worker concurrency.
- Use a hybrid queueing approximation for quick estimates and validate against the sim for edge cases (microbursts, long-tail token distributions).
- Output measures: p50/p95/p99 latency from enqueue->response, GPU utilization, effective tokens/sec, and cost-per-token (amortized GPU + instance overhead).

Key user requirements to satisfy with knobs:
- p95 <= target SLO (e.g., 300ms for short-chat workloads, 2s for long completion workloads).
- Minimize cost-per-token while staying within p95 constraint 95% of the time (we give headroom factor).
- Provide conservative / optimistic recommendations (two-config outputs).

Model assumptions (configurable in spreadsheet):
- Arrival process: support Poisson baseline + configurable burst multiplier + scheduled spikes (to simulate cron or product events). Also allow heavy-tailed interarrival (Weibull-ish) to model user clustering.
- Token lengths: Empirical distribution buckets (1-20, 20-100, 100-512, 512+). Default uses production sample from q4-2024 prompt traces (anonymized).
- Single-request service time (no batching): modeled as function of tokens_out * avg_token_ms + model_latency_overhead (kv cache warm penalty).
- Batch service time: simulated as max(single_request_time for the batch) * batch_factor + batch_kernel_overhead. Batch_factor captures efficient parallel decoding (<= sum of request work).
- Continuous batching window: W ms (when window open, accumulate inflight requests up to max_batch_size).
- Max concurrency per worker: C (number of parallel inferences supported by a single GPU card/process).
- Workers (GPUs) are homogeneous for the sim.
- Network and serialization overhead are additive constants per-request.

Spreadsheet columns / inputs to expose to product teams: (spreadsheet layout notes)
- Workload name, target_p95_ms, expected_rps, arrival_cv (coefficient of variation), burst_pct, mean_tokens_out, token_distribution_percentages, base_gpu_cost_$/hr, workers_reserved, target_gpu_util_pct, batch_window_ms range, max_batch_size, concurrency_per_worker range, preferred_fallback_model (smaller model to failover to)
- Outputs (computed): recommended_concurrency, recommended_batch_window_ms, expected_p95_ms, expected_cost_per_1M_tokens, gpu_utilization, headroom_factor, recommended_reserved_capacity (num gpus)

Simulator pseudocode (high level):
- For t in 0..T step 1ms:
  - generate arrivals for this ms (stochastic according to arrival model)
  - for each arrival: assign token_length from distribution, push into partitioned queue (we partition by batch_key if using routing)
  - every W ms per worker: assemble batch up to max_batch_size from queue, start a batch job with service_time computed as batch_time(tokens_in_batch) / concurrency_factor
  - each worker can run up to C batches in parallel (C is concurrency); if all slots busy, batches wait in queue (this is the slowpath)
  - collect latency per request (enqueue->batch_start + batch_service_time + postproc)
- Record percentiles and utilization

Queueing approximations for fast spreadsheet estimates:
- For steady/low-CV traffic we use an M/G/C approximation with effective service time = mean batch service time under target batch_window and arrival rate.
- Convert to p95 roughly using the heavy-traffic approximation: p95 ~ mean_wait + 1.645 * sqrt(var_wait) + mean_service_time (tune with calibration factor).
- Use conservative fudge factor 1.2 for tail under bursty traffic; switch to full sim for burst_pct > 20% or arrival_cv > 1.5.

Observations from early sim runs (notes):
- Small window (W < 15ms) + high concurrency (C >= 8) gives excellent p95 for latency-sensitive low-token workloads, but increases GPU wasted cycles (util drop) because of more context-switch overhead.
- Large window (W 50-100ms) yields high batch sizes which sharply reduce cost-per-token for long completions but increases p95 significantly for small requests.
- There is a non-linear sweet spot where batch_size * concurrency saturates GPU FLOPs: beyond that, adding either knob yields diminishing returns and increases latency variance.
- Microbursts (short spikes 5x RPS for 1-3s) are the main driver of p95 tail; recommended to provision a small number of prewarmed workers to absorb microbursts rather than raising baseline concurrency across fleet.

Concrete heuristic recommendations (deliverable):
1) For chat-like workloads (short tokens, tight SLO): prefer W in 5-25ms, C 6-12, max_batch_size modest (8-24). Target GPU util 40-65%. Use small headroom_factor 1.15.
2) For completion-heavy workloads (long tokens, high throughput): W 40-120ms, C 2-6, max_batch_size 32-128. Target GPU util 70-90%, headroom_factor 1.05.
3) For mixed/multi-tenant unpredictable traffic: autoscale more frequently, use adaptive window: W = clamp( base_W * sqrt(current_rps/steady_rps), 5, 100 ). Also enable prefix-caching where possible to reduce effective service time.
4) For microbursts: keep 1-2 prewarmed workers per cluster (small instance warm start) or enable grace-period short-circuit to fallback smaller model for bursts.

Cost model summary (spreadsheet cells):
- base_gpu_cost_per_hour = input
- amortized_cost_per_token = (base_gpu_cost_per_hour / (3600 * tokens_per_sec_at_util)) * (1 + infra_overhead_pct)
- tokens_per_sec_at_util derived from sim average tokens/sec per GPU and target util
- show sensitivity table across base_gpu_cost_per_hour +/- 20% and arrival_rps +/- 30%

Validation plan and experiments to run (next 2 weeks):
- Run grid of (W: 5,15,30,60,120) x (C: 2,4,8,16) x (arrival_cv: 0.6,1.0,1.8) x (mean_tokens: 10,80,300) — save p95 and cost per 1M tokens outputs into spreadsheet.
- Compare fast M/G/C estimates to sim for each cell; capture calibration factors for tail fudge.
- Run 10k-sample microburst scenarios to quantify prewarm counts and compute missed-SLO probability.
- Add a column that flags configs where cold-KV-cache penalty > 150ms and mark them as "requires-cache-warmup".

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to properly model multi-model routing (hot-spot models vs fallback models) in cost per token? For now we approximate with weighted average service time. Need product input on fallback ratio expectations.
- Should we expose per-organization default headroom (enterprise customers may want lower headroom if they prefer reserved capacity)? Add policy knob.
- Validate batch_factor numbers vs microbench kernels (coordinate with infra/kernel team).
- Add longer-run 24h sim to capture diurnal and scheduled job interactions.

Action items (owners):
- Aisha: finalize sim code and export CSV interface for spreadsheet (due 2025-01-24).
- Diego: run kernel microbenchmarks for batch_factor calibration (due 2025-01-21).
- Eleni: pull anonymized token-length histogram for new quarterly sample (due 2025-01-18).
- Marcus: wire up small dashboard that reads the grid CSVs and highlights recommended rows (due 2025-02-07).

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic; aim for recommendations that product teams can understand and that can be implemented with existing autoscaler + routing knobs.
- The spreadsheet will have both fast-estimate cells (for quick tradeoffs) and deep-sim CSVs (for final sizing).

Appendix (calibration constants we used during run):
- base_kernel_overhead_ms = 6.5ms
- avg_token_ms_decode = 0.65ms (for model-family-A quantized path)
- batch_factor (empirical) = 0.55 to 0.9 depending on mix; default use 0.7
- cold_kv_cache_penalty_ms = 120ms

End of note.

Quick links (internal):
- simulation notebook: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/tree/main/sims/continuous-batching
- backlog epic: JIRA-RT-3214
- kernel microbench PR: github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pulls/512
summary: Working sim + spreadsheet plan for continuous batching and concurrency sizing. Produces heuristic recs for SLO-driven configs, validation grid, and open action items.
